sections.h2: How does an Illinois tax sale work?
sections.html:
An Illinois tax sale auctions the unpaid property tax on a parcel, not the house itself. After taxes turn delinquent, the county collector must publish a notice of the intended application for judgment and sale, and the notice lists each delinquent property by PIN number and, where available, by address (35 ILCS 200/21-110). The notice runs in a newspaper published in the township or road district, or in a county newspaper when none exists there.

Bidders compete on the penalty. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-215, the person offering to pay the amount due for the least penalty percentage becomes the purchaser, and no bid may exceed a 9% penalty on the tax. The winner receives a certificate of purchase, and the owner keeps title while the redemption clock runs.

A county board may also bid as trustee for the taxing districts, applying the unpaid taxes to the bid so that no cash changes hands (35 ILCS 200/21-90). A county that holds a certificate this way can later sell the property or assign the certificate to a municipality, a land bank or a nonprofit housing developer.

sections.h2: How long does an owner have to redeem?
sections.html:
Property sold at a tax sale may be redeemed any time before 3 years from the date of sale, with listed exceptions, under 35 ILCS 200/21-350. The first exception concerns property that is vacant on the date of sale. The section says the 2024 changes apply to certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, and the 104th General Assembly amendment applies to certificates issued on or after July 10, 2026.

Because the rule depends on the issue date of the certificate, an older sale may run on a shorter schedule. The county clerk can tell you the sale date and the redemption deadline for any parcel. Every redemption period begins on the date of the tax sale, according to section 22-5.

The buyer can lengthen the period by filing a written notice with the county clerk, but only to a date no later than 3 years after the sale, and only with the clerk's date-stamped acknowledgment (35 ILCS 200/21-385). For certificates a county holds as trustee, the clerk may set up a payment plan that waives interest penalties while the owner keeps up with it.

sections.h2: What does it cost to redeem?
sections.html:
You pay the county clerk, not the tax buyer. Section 21-355 requires a deposit in United States money, a cashier's check, a certified check or a qualifying money order payable to the county clerk. It counts as timely only if the clerk's office receives it in person before the close of business on the last day, or if a post office cancellation mark is dated at least one day earlier.

The total has several parts: the certificate amount, an accrued penalty, any later taxes the buyer paid plus a 12% penalty for each year or part of a year, and fees tied to the buyer's court filings and notices. The penalty is a multiple of the penalty bid at the sale, and it steps up every six months.

Ask the clerk for a written redemption figure for the exact day you plan to pay, because the number moves as periods change and as fees are posted.

sections.h2: What notices must a tax buyer send before asking for a deed?
sections.html:
The law makes the tax buyer prove that the owner was warned. Within 4 months and 15 days after the sale, the buyer delivers a notice to the county clerk, who mails it by registered or certified mail to the party in whose name the taxes were last assessed (35 ILCS 200/22-5). The form tells the owner that title and the right to possession may transfer, that a homeowner could eventually face eviction, and that HUD can point to local housing counselors.

  • Between 6 and 3 months before the redemption period ends, the buyer gives a second notice to owners, occupants, the municipality and interested parties such as a mortgagee of record (section 22-10).
  • The petition for a tax deed is filed in circuit court between 6 and 3 months before the period expires (section 22-30).
  • The notice names a hearing date and says the owner may respond or appear and speak to the court.
  • The court is told to insist on strict compliance with sections 22-10 through 22-25.

A missed or defective notice is a real defense, so keep every envelope and letter you receive and give copies to an attorney.

sections.h2: What happens when the redemption period ends?
sections.html:
Since the 2024 amendments, a court that finds the notices proper orders a judicial tax deed auction, and the property is offered to the highest bidder within 120 days of the order (35 ILCS 200/22-40). The tax deed judgment amount includes the redemption figure, the petitioner's later taxes and costs, a capped attorney fee and publication costs. It earns interest at 0.75% per month from the judgment until the auction.

The former owner is not automatically wiped out. The statutory notice tells an owner that money left after taxes and fees are paid may be claimed, and the clerk's tax deed fee comes with a surplus equity fund fee of $500 in counties under 3,000,000 residents and $1,000 in larger ones. Those fees fund the county's surplus equity fund. Deeds issued to a county trustee skip that fee.

A tax deed does not erase every claim, since section 22-45 lets a court void a deed in limited cases. In counties of 3,000,000 or more, a homestead deed can be voided on petition within 3 months of the order if the home was owner occupied and a county employee made a negligent or willful error that the owner relied on.

A scavenger sale is the collector's way to move properties that carry long-running delinquent tax, and section 21-260 sets its rules. Unsold parcels are offered again each year.

  • The minimum bid is $250, or one-half of the tax if the total liability is under $500.
  • A sale is not final until the court confirms it.
  • On confirmation it extinguishes the in rem lien of the general taxes, but the owner's personal liability for the tax remains.
  • The certificate holder may petition for a tax deed within 6 months before the redemption period ends.
  • Redemption after a sale on or after September 9, 1993 carries interest of 3% per month for the first 2 months, then 12%, 24%, 36% and 48% across the later periods, and 6% per year after 24 months.

Except for owner-occupied single-family units, a redemption from a scavenger sale also requires payment of other taxes that were delinquent when the sale occurred.

sections.h2: How should a seller with a tax-sale parcel proceed?
sections.html:
Start by learning where the parcel sits on the timeline, since the answer drives every option.

  • Ask the county collector whether the taxes were sold, and ask the county clerk for the sale date, certificate number and redemption deadline.
  • Request the redemption total in writing and keep the receipt for any deposit.
  • Read each court notice and calendar the hearing date.
  • Tell any title company about the certificate before you sign a contract, because a recorded tax deed is a separate event from a sale you make.
  • Remember that tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under section 31-45, while a voluntary sale by the owner is not.

A buyer who purchases as is and pays cash can close faster than a financed buyer, which matters when the redemption date is close. The redemption itself still has to be made to the county clerk by the deadline.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period after an Illinois tax sale?
faqs.a: For certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, the general period is 3 years from the date of sale under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, with exceptions that begin with vacant property. Ask the county clerk for the deadline on your certificate.

faqs.q: Can I lose my house at an Illinois tax sale?
faqs.a: The sale itself does not move title. The tax buyer must give notices, file a petition and win a court order for a tax deed or judicial tax deed auction after the redemption period passes.
The county clerk. Section 21-355 requires the deposit to be payable to the county clerk and received before the close of business on the last day, or postmarked at least one day earlier.

faqs.q: What is the highest penalty a bidder can offer at an Illinois tax sale?
faqs.a: A bid cannot exceed a 9% penalty on the tax or special assessment, and the bidder offering the lowest penalty percentage wins under section 21-215.

faqs.q: Is a tax deed subject to the Illinois transfer tax?
faqs.a: No. Tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-45, although a voluntary sale by an owner is taxed at the state rate.
